column1: # When the thing you typed is itself a word -- just a much rarer one.
# Drop the last letter of "contrast" and you have written "contras", which is
# in the dictionary at rank 49,136 while "contrast" sits at 3,862.  For a long
# time the exact match won anyway, because base_exact stood 26 points above
# base_prefix and the frequency term spans only 34 points across the whole
# corpus -- so no completion, however common, could ever overtake a word you
# The cost of being wrong here is symmetric: whichever reading loses sits at
# rank 2, one keystroke away.  So the commoner one should lead, and these cases
# pin that in both directions, because bench/evaluate.lua cannot see any of it
# -- its generated inputs are misspellings, and a misspelling that lands on
# another real word is exactly what the generator filters out.
# The blockers below are a mixture on purpose.  Some are real English (`wit`,
# why this is fixed in the ranking rather than by deleting entries: a filter
# aggressive enough to remove `trave` also removes `wit`.
# And the word you typed is still right there, one key away.  This half is the
# guard: it is what stops anyone "fixing" the cases above by lowering
# base_exact until the exact match stops mattering at all.
# The other direction, which is the failure this trades against.  A rare word
# that nothing much commoner completes must still lead, or typing an ordinary
# word stops working.  `tat` and `rom` are the historical pair: raising
# base_exact once made every rare word unbeatable, and lowering it too far
# Contractions are the deliberate exception and stay as they were: the bare
# word is a word in its own right and comes first, with the contraction
